urgency.eyebrow: What the Property Owner Is Doing Right Now
urgency.h: The Spill Was Cleaned Up in Minutes. The Footage Is Next.
urgency.sub: You didn't ask to get hurt buying groceries. But the store's insurer has a checklist — and it starts with making the hazard disappear.

cards.p: Most business cameras loop every 7–30 days. The video that shows the puddle sat there for an hour — and nobody put out a cone — is gone unless a lawyer demands it now.

cards.t: The incident report is their document
cards.p: The manager who was so concerned wrote a report for the insurance company, not for you. "Customer stated she wasn't looking where she was going" is a classic. Don't sign, don't guess — call us.

cards.t: They will call it your fault
cards.p: "Open and obvious." "Wrong shoes." "Wasn't paying attention." Premises cases turn on proving the owner knew — or should have known — about the hazard. We know how to prove it.

result_highlight: Under California law, property owners must inspect for hazards and fix or warn about them. When a grocery store, landlord, or hotel skips that duty and someone gets hurt, they owe medical bills, lost wages, and pain and suffering. In 2024 we secured 59 of the state's top 100 injury settlements.

value.h: A Fall Can Change Everything. So Can a Case.
value.sub: Broken hips, wrists, and backs. Concussions. For older adults, a fall can be life-altering. California law says the owner pays for all of it.

items.t: Every medical bill — past and future
items.p: ER, imaging, surgery, hardware, physical therapy, and the follow-up care years from now. Priced by medical experts, not by the store's adjuster.
The work you missed while healing — and the work you can't do anymore if the injury is permanent.
Chronic pain, limited mobility, the independence you lost. No cap on these damages in most California injury cases.
If you needed help at home — a caregiver, a family member who took time off, mobility equipment — that's part of the claim.
If a fall took someone you love, the family can recover funeral costs, lost support, and the loss of companionship and care.

faq.q: Do I really have a case just from falling?
faq.a: If you fell because of a hazard the owner knew about or should have found — a spill, a broken step, poor lighting, an uneven walkway, ice, debris — and you were hurt, yes. The question is what they knew and when. That's what the footage and maintenance logs show, and it's why we act fast.

faq.q: I didn't report it to the store when it happened.
faq.a: You can still have a case. Go get medical care, write down everything you remember, keep the shoes and clothes you were wearing, and call us. We'll figure out how to document it.

faq.q: The store's insurer offered to pay my medical bills.
faq.a: Don't sign anything. That offer almost always comes with a release of every claim you have — including the pain, lost work, and future care they're not mentioning. Get a free review first.

faq.q: How long do I have to file?
I fell on city property. Is that different?
faq.a: Yes — and urgently. Claims against a city, county, or state agency generally must be filed within six months. If you fell on a public sidewalk, in a park, or at a government building, call today.
Nothing up front — ever. We front every cost of building your case and only collect a fee if we recover money for you. No recovery, no attorney fee.
